parsed.same_study_reason: Both lists describe an intervention with micro/informal enterprises, tax-payment outcomes, tax-official visits, economic-activity measures, and a 2SLS knowledge mechanism.

pairs.reason: Both concern validity of the tax-payment outcome. A1 focuses on missing receipt amounts coded as zero, whereas B6 focuses on treatment-induced differential classification or reporting of what counts as a tax payment.

Both identify the receipt-based tax-revenue measure and the coding of missing or unverified receipt values as zero. Both say this conflates non-verification with nonpayment and makes the revenue result sensitive to missing-data assumptions.

Both concern economic-activity outcomes collected in endline surveys and the risk that differential engagement by enumerators affects reporting. A2 is more explicit about respondent familiarity and trust, while B2 also notes seasonality and survey timing.

Both challenge the 2SLS knowledge-treatment interpretation because assignment can affect outcomes through channels other than measured knowledge, violating the exclusion restriction. B3 adds concerns about the constructed knowledge measure.

Both question attribution of outcomes to information or knowledge rather than other treatment pathways. A2 identifies rapport with the shared enumeration team and its implications for the IV exclusion restriction; B4 identifies unequal training and follow-up attention as a Hawthorne or attention mechanism.

Both concern the tax-official visit variable. A3 asks whether treatment changes the probability of a visit, while B5 identifies bias from conditioning or splitting analyses on this post-treatment variable.

Both say the observed tax-enforcement or visit pattern cannot substantiate the proposed mechanism without a direct test. A3 broadly asks whether treatment affects visit likelihood; B9 narrows this to claimed reallocation of audits across revenue groups and calls for administrative enforcement data.
